EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  
“Trade‐Liberalization and Firm Productivity: Evidence from Indonesia, 1991-2001”  

====================================================================  
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Strategy: Difference-in-Differences with continuous treatment intensity, complemented by an event-study specification for pre-trend tests.

Rationale  
• The key reform—large cuts in tariffs on intermediate inputs—varied in timing and depth across 4-digit ISIC industries.  
• We observe the same firms before and after the reform, so firm fixed effects purge time-invariant unobservables.  
• Year fixed effects net out macro shocks (e.g. Asian crisis).  
• Identification therefore comes from differential changes in input tariffs across industries over time.  
• A generalized DID (sometimes called “two-way fixed effects with continuous treatment”) is standard in the trade-productivity literature and easily extended to an event-study to inspect dynamics and pre-trends.

====================================================================  
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
Tariff_it: statutory ad-valorem tariff on intermediate inputs faced by firm f in industry i at time t.  
Implementation:  
  Step 1. Obtain tariff schedule at HS-6 or HS-8 level.  
  Step 2. Map HS products to ISIC industries via the Indonesian 1990 input–output table.  
  Step 3. Construct an industry-level, input-weighted tariff: τ_it = Σ_h w_ih,1990 * Tariff_ht, where weights w are the share of input h in industry i’s 1990 intermediate expenditures (pre-period weights avoid endogeneity).  
  Step 4. Merge τ_it to firms by their primary ISIC code.

“Treatment” = larger decline in τ_it after 1995 (the core reform years).  
Control group  
Industries whose input tariffs change little or not at all over the same period provide the counterfactual trend. This is a “many-to-many” control; no separate explicit control group is necessary, but firms in low-change industries implicitly serve as controls.  

Timing  
Define Post_t = 1 for years ≥ the first large cut in the firm’s industry (industry-specific first-difference of ≥ ‑5 p.p. between t-1 and t, or simply use calendar year dummy as in baseline). Event-study will use k = (t – reform year_i).  

(We do not use an RDD, so no running variable/cutoff.)

====================================================================  
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel Trends: Absent tariff cuts, productivity trends would have been parallel across industries with high vs. low tariff reductions.  
  – Plausibility: Indonesia’s reform was centrally designed, not targeted at “struggling” sectors, and covered virtually all manufacturing. We will test this via pre-trend coefficients in the event-study.  

A2. No Anticipation: Firms did not change productivity in advance of announced tariff reductions.  
  – Plausibility: Tariff schedules were often negotiated with little advance notice; still, we check for “leads” of treatment.  

A3. Stable Composition: Entry/exit or reclassification is not systematically driven by unobserved productivity shocks correlated with tariff changes.  
  – Plausibility: The census tracks incumbents and entrants; we will show results on balanced and unbalanced panels separately.  

A4. Exogeneity of Tariff Changes: Within‐industry tariff changes are not set in response to contemporaneous, unobserved productivity shocks.  
  – Plausibility: Reform was negotiated internationally (ASEAN and WTO) and politically driven; still, we control for industry*year exports/imports pre-trend and allow industry-specific linear time trends.  

====================================================================  
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Differential Industry Shocks (e.g. technology trends)  
  • Mitigation: Add industry-specific linear or quadratic trends; include controls for world-price shocks (import-weighted world price index).  

T2. Measurement Error in Tariffs (HS-to-ISIC mapping)  
  • Mitigation: Weight tariffs with fixed 1990 IO shares; conduct robustness using alternative mappings (e.g. UN concordance) and using firm-specific input mix if available.  

T3. Simultaneous Output-Tariff Cuts (final-good liberalization)  
  • Mitigation: Control for output tariff τ_output_it in all regressions; interact with Post to allow different effects.  

====================================================================  
5. R CODE OUTLINE (executable)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast TWFE & event study
library(ggplot2)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data Loading
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Assume four CSVs: firm panel, tariff schedule, IO weights, HS-ISIC concordance
firm  <- fread("indo_firm_1991_2001.csv")        # id, year, isic4, output, inputs, tfp
tariff<- fread("tariff_hs_1990_2001.csv")        # hs6, year, tariff_rate
io    <- fread("io_weights_1990.csv")            # isic4, hs6, weight
concd <- fread("hs_to_isic4.csv")                # hs6, isic4

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct Industry-Year Input Tariff
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Merge tariff with concordance & IO weights
tariff_isic <- merge(tariff, concd, by="hs6")
tariff_isic <- merge(tariff_isic, io, by=c("isic4","hs6"))

# weight tariff by 1990 IO shares
tariff_isic[, wt_tariff := tariff_rate * weight]

# aggregate to industry-year
tau_it <- tariff_isic[, .(input_tariff = sum(wt_tariff)), by=.(isic4, year)]

# OPTIONAL: output tariffs
out_tariff <- fread("output_tariff_isic_year.csv")   # isic4, year, output_tariff

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Merge with Firm Data
# ------------------------------------------------------------
panel <- merge(firm, tau_it,  by=c("isic4","year"))
panel <- merge(panel, out_tariff, by=c("isic4","year"), all.x=TRUE)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Create Treatment Intensity & Event-time
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Identify first large cut per industry (>5 p.p. drop)
tau_it[, d_tau := input_tariff - shift(input_tariff), by=isic4]
reform_year <- tau_it[d_tau <= -5, .SD[1], by=isic4][, .(isic4, reform_year = year)]

panel <- merge(panel, reform_year, by="isic4", all.x=TRUE)
panel[, event_time := year - reform_year]      # negative=pre, 0=reform

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Baseline TWFE Regression
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# (log TFP or Levinsohn-Petrin measure saved as ln_tfp)
est_baseline <- feols(ln_tfp ~ input_tariff + output_tariff | id + year,
                      data = panel, cluster = ~isic4)
summary(est_baseline)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Event-Study (dynamic effects & pre-trends)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
panel[, event_grp := fifelse(event_time <= -4, -4,
                      fifelse(event_time >= 5, 5, event_time))]
est_es <- feols(ln_tfp ~ i(event_grp, ref=-1) + output_tariff |
                id + year, data=panel, cluster=~isic4)
iplot(est_es)      # displays dynamic coefficients

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Robustness: Balanced Panel (firms observed ≥8 yrs)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
keep_ids <- panel[, .N, by=id][N >= 8]$id
panel_bal <- panel[id %in% keep_ids]

est_bal <- feols(ln_tfp ~ input_tariff + output_tariff | id + year,
                 data = panel_bal, cluster = ~isic4)
summary(est_bal)
```

====================================================================  
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Economic theory (Melitz-type models with imported inputs) predicts that cheaper intermediates raise firm-level productivity through learning, variety, and quality channels. We therefore expect:  
• Direction: β < 0 (because higher tariff ⇒ lower productivity). Equivalently, a one-percentage-point tariff decrease should increase productivity.  
• Magnitude: Prior studies (e.g. Amiti & Konings 2007 on the same reform) find roughly 0.012–0.02 log-productivity increase per 1 p.p. tariff cut. We expect a similar range: β ≈ −0.015.  

====================================================================  
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Parallel trends visually & statistically supported (event-study) .............. 1  
C2: No anticipation (leads insignificant) ......................................... 1  
C3: Correct functional form/no heterogeneous timing bias (use event-study & Sun-Abraham) .......................................................................... 0.5  
C4: No spillovers/contamination across industries .................................. 0.5  
C5: Appropriate inference (cluster ≥50 industries) ................................ 1  
TOTAL (max 5) = 4.0  

====================================================================
